body:
You are drafting DIALOGUE TEXT for a video game. Reply in plain text only, in exactly the format asked at the end.

"The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG (think Baldur's Gate 3: fully voiced, branching dialogue, skill checks, a storyteller Narrator). It is folk horror set in Druskenvald, an afterlife realm of endless night under a gargantuan crescent moon with a leering crone's face; an autumn that never ends, pumpkins and bonfires and dead leaves everywhere, but the stakes are real. Humour is deadpan and sits beside the dread. Use only the names given here; invent no new named people, places, monsters or history.

THE PARTY: the player leads four heroes; never name, describe or gender the player's heroes. Some of the party may be these companions, who speak only in the `interject` lines written for them (each line is said only if that companion is present, so it must make sense on its own and never answer another companion's line):
- rook_coldwake: Rook, a Graveborn (undead) fighter, a graveyard rest warden; dry, level, practical, union-minded, cares that the dead are laid to rest properly; few words.
- tobin_hayward: Tobin, a Harvestborn (living scarecrow of wicker and straw) druid; brisk, warm, country-wise, talks about rot, roots, harvests and neighbours; kind under the sharp tongue.
- silas_vane: Silas, a Relicborn (skeleton-folk) monk and card sharp from river landings; fast, cocky, thinks in odds, bets and marks.
- delphine_ravelle: Delphine, a Threadborn (living patchwork doll) warlock; theatrical vaudeville showwoman, says "darling", treats horror as a third-rate sideshow she means to headline.
- lucan_houndstooth: Lucan, a Curseborn (wolf-man) ranger and monster hunter; hushed and earnest, narrates danger like a nature broadcaster, notices scents and tracks.
- cordelia_skein: Cordelia, a Silkborn (spider-folk) sorcerer; cool, cultivated, clinical, delighted by anything morbid as a subject of study.

RULES FOR THE TEXT
- Spoken lines: 1 to 3 short sentences, about 12 to 30 words, never over 40. Contractions are normal. People talk in their own voice and do not explain the plot to the audience. Accent is word choice and rhythm, never phonetic spelling. Country folk of the Hollow speak with a folksy country drawl in their word choice.
- Interject lines: one sentence, under 20 words.
- Option lines (what the player's party says or does): under 12 words, plain, in the party's voice ("We..." or an imperative).
- Narrator lines (the Vagrant, an old train conductor telling the tale afterwards: warm, folksy, wry, a Southern drawl in word choice such as reckon, ain't, folks, a spell, a piece; drop a final g in at most one line in three): second person, present tense, one or two sentences, only what a hero could perceive, concrete senses (smell, sound, texture, cold), no game words (HP, roll, level, check, DC, save, hit points), never tell the player what to feel, never the word "suddenly", never mention a fiddle, never name the Vagrant.
- No stage directions, asterisks, italics, brackets, placeholders, emoji or em dashes (use commas, periods, colons). Straight quotes only. Do not use the arrow characters -> or => inside the text.
- Content is dark but restrained: no gore, no graphic detail.
- Each brief says what the line must do; keep its facts, write it as the speaker would say it.

THIS SCENE: short meetings on the roads of Wickermoor Hollow in Act I, played while the party travels between places on the map. The party arrived by the Ghostlight Express, a ghost train that carries the dead; tonight a shade sabotaged it and it came down in an oak wood, and its dead passengers are scattered, some lost, some turned grey and hostile by the Shroud (a devouring white mist). The nearest town is Wickermoor Village, a timber-framed village round a square with an oak of carved faces. Most villagers follow the Old Ways and worship the Green Queen (a leafy woman's face on their shrines; once a kindly mother of the wood; something has gone wrong with her that nobody says aloud, and a few whisper about "the crooked one"). The Brightsingers are newer settlers who dress bright, carry lanterns, sing hymns to the sun and are building a church. On the hill above the village stands the Druskenvald Estate, a pretty manor where Lord Phillip and Lady Adela Druskenvald have invited the party to dinner; its windows sometimes light on the wrong floors.

Speakers (besides the Narrator and the companions above):
- road_passenger: a dead woman passenger from the Ghostlight Express, in a travelling coat and hat, a ticket in her hand, see-through at the edges; polite, anxious, from somewhere far away; she does not know she is dead and that the train crashed.
- road_bonfire_keeper: an old Old Ways farmer who tends a bonfire of animal bones where two tracks cross on the moor, to keep the Shroud off the road; friendly, slow, a little too interested in what travellers give the fire.
- joan_murdoch: Joan Murdoch, a Brightsinger missionary, the preacher's wife; beaming, warm, relentlessly hopeful; she walks the hill road with lanterns and hymns.

The meetings (the [[n]] markers in this file are yours; everything else is fixed):

```
# --- The Green Queen's shrine ---

~ wayside_shrine
set road_shrine_met
Narrator: [[53]]
interject name:tobin_hayward: [[54]]
interject name:silas_vane: [[55]]
-> ws_menu

~ ws_menu
* [if gold >= 2] [[56]] -> ws_offer
* [[57]] -> ws_take
* [if not flag.road_shrine_read] [Religion DC 13] [[58]] -> ws_read | ws_read_fail
* [[59]] -> END

~ ws_offer
gold -2
Narrator: [[60]]
hit_dice restore 1 party
-> END

~ ws_take
set road_shrine_robbed
gold +6
Narrator: [[61]]
disadvantage checks 1h: [[62]]
approve tobin_hayward -2 silas_vane +1: You emptied the Green Queen's offering bowl
-> END

~ ws_read
set road_shrine_read
Narrator: [[63]]
Narrator: [[64]]
-> ws_menu

~ ws_read_fail
set road_shrine_read
Narrator: [[65]]
-> ws_menu

# --- The Brightsingers' lantern walk (the hill road) ---

~ lantern_walk
set road_lanterns_met
appear joan_murdoch
Narrator: [[66]]
joan_murdoch [smile]: [[67]]
interject name:delphine_ravelle: [[68]]
-> lw_menu

~ lw_menu
* [Performance DC 12] [[69]] -> lw_sing | lw_sing_flat
* [if not flag.road_lanterns_asked] [[70]] -> lw_ask
* [[71]] -> lw_leave

~ lw_sing
Narrator: [[72]]
joan_murdoch [smile]: [[73]]
bless party 2h
approve delphine_ravelle +1 tobin_hayward +1: You sang with the Brightsingers on the hill road
-> END

~ lw_sing_flat
Narrator: [[74]]
joan_murdoch [smile]: [[75]]
-> END

~ lw_ask
set road_lanterns_asked
joan_murdoch: [[76]]
joan_murdoch [afraid]: [[77]]
-> lw_menu

~ lw_leave
joan_murdoch [smile]: [[78]]
-> END
```

Briefs for the markers:
53. narrator: in the hollow of an old oak by the road sits a little shrine: a carved woman's face crowned with leaves, a bowl of coins, a rotten apple and a rag doll
54. interject tobin_hayward: the Green Queen's face; my mother kept one by the door, though she never would say what it was for
55. interject silas_vane: there's a bowl of honest money there with nobody minding it; I'm only saying
56. option: leave two gold pieces in the bowl
57. option: take the coins
58. option: study the carving
59. option: leave it be
60. narrator: the coins clink in among the others and a breath of warm air comes out of the oak, smelling of cut hay; the ache of the road eases out of your legs
61. narrator: the coins are cold, colder than they ought to be; when you straighten up the carved face seems to have turned a fraction to watch you
62. the reason shown for a penalty on the party's checks for an hour, three to six words, about the shrine's eyes on them
63. narrator: under the moss the face is older than the leaves around it; the leaves were cut later, by a different hand, over something like a crown of twigs, bent and crooked
64. narrator: someone has scratched a line under the face more recently, deep and careful: a crooked smile
65. narrator: it's an old carving of a woman in leaves and that's all it'll tell you tonight
66. narrator: lanterns come bobbing up the hill road in a line, three women and a boy in bright yellow and sky blue, singing a hymn about the sun coming back
67. joan_murdoch: friends, join us! they walk the hill road every night to keep the dark honest; one more voice and the sun hears them better
68. interject delphine_ravelle: a choir in the dark with lanterns; darling, that's practically my first booking
69. option: sing along with them
70. option: ask about the manor on the hill
71. option: wish them well and go on
72. narrator: your voices go up with theirs, and for a verse the lanterns burn brighter and the hill doesn't feel so tall
73. joan_murdoch: oh, beautiful! she says they carry a little of the sun with them now, she promises
74. narrator: the tune gets away from you halfway through and never comes back; the boy giggles behind his lantern
75. joan_murdoch: kindly, the sun doesn't mind a flat note, friend, only a silent one
76. joan_murdoch: the Lord and Lady are lovely people, generous to the church; it's only the house; Brightsingers don't sing past the gate
77. joan_murdoch: her smile slips; she has seen candles lit in rooms on floors the house doesn't have; then she laughs it off
78. joan_murdoch: go with the light, friends, and keep to the road
Also write the narration that starts each road fight (Narrator lines, the same rules):
79. two pale haints, the restless dead from the wreck, drift out of the fog toward your warmth, mouths open
80. three haints come out of the heather, and behind them a dead passenger gone grey and wrong, still dragging a suitcase
81. eyes in the bracken, a dozen of them, low to the ground: weasels, chittering and sniffing at your mouths as if they smell your teeth
82. a weasel big as a hound leads the pack out of the heather, with eyes too knowing for any animal
83. passengers from the wreck come shambling down the road with their luggage, faces grey as the mist that got into them
84. hares sit up in the road ahead, too long in the leg, too many teeth in their grins, and they do not run
85. a magpie on a fencepost counts you, one for sorrow, two for joy, and does not like the number; the sky fills with wings
86. wolves have been pacing you on the far side of the hedge for a mile; now they stop pretending
87. weasels pour across the hill road like spilt ink, sniffing and chittering, and turn their noses toward you all at once
88. hares in the ruts of the hill road, grinning, ears laid back, and they come at you instead of running
89. magpies settle on the oak branches over the hill road one by one until the branches bow; then they drop

## Reply format
One line per marker, in order, exactly `n => text` (no quotes around the text, no extra lines, no commentary). 37 lines, numbered as above.
result:
53 => Tucked in the hollow of an old roadside oak sits a little shrine: a woman's face carved in leaves, a bowl of coins, a soft brown apple, and a limp rag doll.
54 => That's the Green Queen's face, sure enough, though Mother never would say why we kept one by the door.
55 => That's a bowl of honest coin sitting there with nobody minding it, if you catch my drift.
56 => Drop two gold pieces into the offering bowl.
57 => Pocket the coins from the bowl.
58 => Look closer at the carved wooden face.
59 => Leave the shrine be and move on.
60 => Your coins clink into the bowl, and a warm breath of fresh-cut hay sighs out of the hollow trunk. The road-ache eases right out of your legs.
61 => Those coins bite your palm like river ice. When you straighten up, you could swear that wooden face has turned a fraction to watch you go.
62 => The carved eyes follow your steps
63 => Under the damp moss, the face is older than the leaves around it. A second hand carved that foliage later to cover a bent, crooked crown of twigs.
64 => Someone took a sharp blade to the wood not long ago, cutting a deep, careful line beneath the chin: a crooked smile.
65 => It's just an old carving of a woman crowned in leaves, and reckon that's all it's tellin' you tonight.
66 => Warm lanterns come bobbing up the hill road in a neat line. Three women and a boy in bright yellow and sky blue are singing a hymn for the sun's return.
67 => Friends, come walk with us a spell! We sing the hill road every night to keep the dark honest, and one more voice helps the sun hear us plain.
68 => A lantern choir in the dead of night, darling, that's practically my first booking in this dreary province.
69 => Join in and sing the hymn with them.
70 => Ask them about the manor up on the hill.
71 => Wish them well and keep walking.
72 => Your voices rise with theirs into the cold air, and for a verse or two the lantern flames burn taller and the steep hill don't seem half so long.
73 => Oh, now wasn't that lovely! You carry a little piece of the sun with you down the road tonight, I promise you that.
74 => The tune slips away from you halfway through the verse and never comes back. Behind his brass lantern, the boy hides a giggle in his sleeve.
75 => Bless your hearts, the sun doesn't mind a flat note, friend. It only minds a silent one.
76 => Lord Phillip and Lady Adela are fine, generous souls who gave good timber for our church. It's only the house itself: we Brightsingers don't sing past the iron gate.
77 => I've looked up from this road and seen candles burning in windows on floors that house doesn't even have. Mind me, jumping at lamplight like a silly goose!
78 => Go with the light, friends, and keep your boots to the road.
79 => Two pale haints from the train wreck drift out of the cold fog toward the warmth of your breath, their mouths open wide and silent.
80 => Three restless haints rise out of the frostbitten heather, and behind them shambles a dead passenger gone grey with the mist, still draggin' a leather suitcase.
81 => A dozen wet, dark eyes glitter low in the bracken. Weasels creep out onto the track, chittering sharp and sniffing upward like they can smell the teeth in your head.
82 => A weasel big as a hound parts the dry heather at the head of its pack, fixing you with dark eyes far too knowing for any beast.
83 => Lost souls from the wreck come shuffling down the ruts with their coats torn and their luggage in hand, their faces grey as the mist curling out of their collars.
84 => Three long-legged hares sit upright in the middle of the road, showing way too many teeth in their grins, and they ain't runnin' from you.
85 => A lone magpie on a fencepost eyes your party, caws once, and reckon he don't care for the count. The night sky above the road goes black with beating wings.
86 => Grey wolves have been pacing you behind the blackthorn hedge for a quiet mile. Now they step out into the road and quit pretending.
87 => Weasels pour across the ruts of the hill road like spilt black ink, chittering low, before every wet nose snaps around toward you at once.
88 => Long hares crouch in the wagon ruts ahead, ears pinned flat and mouths stretched in wet grins, and they bound straight at your throats instead of the brush.
89 => Magpies settle one by one along the oak boughs over the hill road until the heavy wood groans and bows, and then the whole flock drops.
